anchor: One night when all the battlements
title: The poem: Bâkî's qasida for Süleyman
greek: Arabic qaṣīda; Turkish kaside
short: A panegyric qasida to Sultan Süleyman I, usually placed first in Bâkî's Divan; Gibb translated it whole in 1882 and again in 1904.
body: Bâkî (Mahmud Abdülbâki, 1526-1600), the son of a muezzin, became the leading lyric poet of Süleyman's court and was later called 'sultan of poets'. Gibb's heading gives the opening as 'Hengâm-ı şeb ki kungure-i çarh-ı âsmân' ('at the hour of night when the battlements of the wheel of heaven...'). Gibb says this qasida is usually placed first in collections of Bâkî's poems and is 'a perfect example of the form': a long mono-rhymed poem of praise that moves through fixed stages. Here the exordium (nesîb or teşbîb) is a starry night in which the seven planets appear one by one; then comes the turn to the sultan (girizgâh), the praise (medhiye), an inset ghazel (tegazzül), the poet's signature couplet and a closing prayer (duâ). Gibb's second version (1904) differs in many lines and is worth comparing. The archive text is the 1882 version.

title: Heaven as a fortified palace
greek: Persian kungura ('battlement'); Turkish kungure
short: The sky is pictured as a fortress or palace whose battlements are lit with star-lamps, as for a royal festival.
body: The opening image turns the night sky into a palace (Gibb's 1904 version says 'heaven's sublime seray', glossing seray as 'palace') whose crenellations are hung with lamps. Ottoman cities were illuminated (donanma) for royal victories and festivals, and the conceit makes the whole cosmos keep holiday for the sultan before the poet reveals why. The heavens of the poem are those of Ptolemaic astronomy as Muslim poets knew it: nine concentric spheres, from the sphere of the Moon up to the starless Empyrean. Gibb lists them in his notes and adds the conventional personifications that the next couplets use: the Moon a fair youth or girl, Mercury a scribe, Venus a woman musician, the Sun a sovereign, Mars a warrior, Jupiter a judge or vizier, Saturn an old man.

title: The Milky Way: the 'straw-bearers' road'
greek: Persian kāh-kashān ('straw-dragger'); Turkish kehkeşân
short: The Persian name for the Milky Way means the path of the straw-carriers, a trail of chaff spilled across the sky.
body: Gibb's 1904 version keeps the Persian picture: 'the Straw-bearers' Way', and his note explains that keh-keşân, 'the straw-bearers', is the Persian name for what English calls the Milky Way. The image is of chaff dropped along a road by carriers of straw. The same band of light returns later in the panegyric, where the spotted night sky is a leopard held on the chain of the Milky Way. Here, at the start, it simply completes the illuminated field of heaven.

title: Mercury, the scribe of heaven
greek: Arabic ʿUṭārid (the planet Mercury); Turkish nişancı ('tracer of the royal cipher')
short: Mercury, the planet of writers, appears as heaven's chancery secretary, taking up a meteor for a pen to sign God's decrees.
body: In astrological convention Mercury is the planet of scribes and secretaries. Gibb's 1904 version calls him 'The Scribe of heaven' and 'The Cipherer of His decrees', and his note explains that the Cipherer (nişancı) was the Ottoman official who traced the sultan's tuğra, the calligraphic royal monogram, on decrees. So the cosmos is pictured as an Ottoman chancery: God issues commands, Mercury countersigns them with a shooting star for a reed pen, and 'men and jinns obey'. Each of the seven planets is given its traditional office in turn, Moon, Mercury, Venus, Sun, Mars, Jupiter, Saturn, in the order of their spheres.

title: Venus the minstrel, the Sun the tambourine-player
greek: Arabic al-Zuhara (Venus); Persian dāyira or def ('tambourine')
short: Venus plays at the heavenly banquet; the round Sun, pictured as a tambourine-player, has hidden her face below the horizon, since it is night.
body: Venus (Zühre) is conventionally a woman musician, so at the 'banquet of the sky' she plays the harp or lute. The Sun is usually a king, but Gibb notes that here she is a tambourinist, because the solar disc is round like a tambourine and seems to spin as a player spins her instrument on a finger. The Sun is absent because it is night: she has hidden her face 'neath the vaulted sphere'. Gibb's 1882 note refers the reader to a further note on the Sun's sex when personified. The detail prepares the climax of the exordium, when the Sun rises after all.

title: Mars, Jupiter and Saturn
greek: Arabic Mirrīkh (Mars), Mushtarī (Jupiter), Zuḥal (Saturn); Turkish fil-bân ('elephant-keeper')
short: The outer planets take their offices: Mars a swordsman, Jupiter a wise counsellor, Saturn on the seventh sphere a dark old Indian mahout.
body: Mars, the Lesser Infortune, is the warrior with a golden blade. Jupiter, the Greater Fortune and most auspicious planet, sits like a vizier or judge pondering affairs by candlelight. Saturn, the Greater Infortune, highest and slowest of the seven, is an old man on the seventh sphere; Gibb notes that he is often called the elephant-driver of the heavens and is figured as an Indian because he is inauspicious and therefore dark. Gibb's 1904 version makes him 'an Indian watchman, old and grey'. The list of planets is complete just as the poet asks what this pageant means.

title: The rising Sun as Solomon's seal: the turn to the sultan
greek: Arabic khātam Sulaymān; Turkish mühr-i Süleyman; girizgâh ('place of escape')
short: The sun rises like Solomon's seal-ring, and the riddle is solved: the cosmos is decked out for Sultan Süleyman. This couplet is the qasida's girizgâh.
body: In Islamic legend the prophet-king Solomon (Süleyman) ruled jinn, winds and beasts through a seal-ring engraved with the Name of God (the Qur'an speaks of his command over jinn and birds). The sunrise is compared to that seal, and Gibb notes the double reference to Solomon and to the sultan who bore his name. The couplets that follow are what Gibb calls the guriz-gâh, 'the place of flight', where the poet passes from the exordium to the panegyric: the planets' festival was a display of the 'might and fortune of the King who earth doth sway'. The sequence of night, then dawn, then the king, is a compliment in itself: Süleyman is the sun that the stars were waiting for.

title: Jemshid, Darius, Khusrev, Iskender
greek: Persian Jamshīd, Dārā, Khusraw (Arabic Kisrā); Arabic Iskandar
short: Süleyman is matched with the model kings of Persian legend and history: Jemshid in feasting, Darius in war, Khusrev in justice, Alexander in conquest.
body: These are the stock royal exemplars of Persian and Ottoman panegyric, known chiefly through Firdawsī's Shāhnāma and the Alexander romances. Jemshid (Cemşîd), the legendary king of the golden age, owned the world-revealing cup and is the type of royal festivity. Darius (Dârâ) is the last Achaemenid king, defeated by Alexander, here simply the type of a warrior king. Khusrev (Hüsrev) is a Sasanian king; Gibb's 1904 version says 'Kisra', which he identifies as Anushirvan, the type of a just king. Iskender, Alexander the Great, is the world-conqueror. Gibb's note 174 explains Keyâni (from the legendary Kayanian dynasty) as meaning simply 'imperial'. The 1904 version also adds 'Darius of the age' in the next line.

anchor: Prince of the Epoch! Sultan Süleymân!
title: Sultan Süleyman I
greek: Turkish Kanunî ('the Lawgiver'); Süleyman = Solomon
short: Süleyman I (r. 1520-66), called in Turkish the Lawgiver and in Europe the Magnificent, was Bâkî's patron for most of his career.
body: The panegyric piles title on title: Lord of East and West, King of Kings, Prince of the Epoch. Under Süleyman the empire reached its widest extent, and Gibb's notes on this poem remark that Ottoman poetry also reached its highest point in his reign. Bâkî is said to have entered court circles with a qasida presented to the sultan on his return from the Nakhchivan campaign (dated August 1555 in the Turkish encyclopedia entry; some popular sources say 1554); whether that qasida is this one is not stated in the sources consulted here, and readers should not assume it. Bâkî's later Elegy on Sultan Süleyman (also in the archive with its own notes) mourns the same king after his death at Szigetvár in 1566.

title: The leopard-sky in chains
greek: Persian palang ('leopard')
short: The spotted night sky is a leopard; anyone who rebelled against the sultan would be chained like it, the Milky Way serving as its chain.
body: Gibb's note explains that the starry sky is compared to a spotted leopard ('pard' is the old poetic word for leopard), held by the band of the Milky Way as by a chain. The two translations take the couplet differently: in 1882 it is a conditional threat (anyone who rebelled would be bound like the sky), while in 1904 the sky itself 'had made revolt' and been dragged to the sultan as a captive. The difference shows how compressed the original is. Either way the hyperbole is cosmic: even the heavens are subject to the sultan's chain.

title: Spring the perfumer, Autumn the merchant
greek: Persian bahār ('spring'), khazān ('autumn'); ʿaṭṭār ('perfumer'), tājir ('merchant')
short: The seasons are tradesmen in the sultan's service: Spring, a perfume-seller, longs for the scent of his grace; Autumn, scattering gold, still needs his bounty.
body: Gibb explains that Autumn is a rich merchant (in 1904, 'householder') who scatters gold, the yellow leaves, on every side, yet even he needs the sultan's generosity. Spring, which makes the world fragrant, is a perfumer who envies the 'odour' of the sultan's grace. Personified seasons are common in Ottoman verse (Gibb mentions the allegory of King Winter and King Spring elsewhere in his notes). The couplet belongs to the medhiye's praise of royal generosity, which follows the praise of justice and precedes that of the sultan's wrath.

sources.cite: E. J. W. Gibb, Ottoman Poems Translated into English Verse in the Original Forms (London: Trübner, 1882), note 175, p. 253
E. J. W. Gibb, A History of Ottoman Poetry, vol. III (London: Luzac, 1904), ch. on Bâkî, Gibb's footnotes to the qasida

title: Only the music laments
greek: Arabic ḥusn-i taʿlīl ('fine explanation of a cause')
short: No one groans under tyranny in this reign; if flute and lute still 'wail', they are breaking the sultan's law.
body: The plaintive tones of the reed-flute (ney) and lute were heard as weeping. Bâkî turns this into a compliment: so complete is the sultan's justice that the only 'wailing' left in the land is the music's, and that is an offence against his law. This is the figure Ottoman rhetoric called hüsn-i ta'lîl, inventing a fanciful cause for a natural fact; Gibb points out the same figure in the inset ghazel, where flowers bend in the wind and the poet says they bow in worship.

sources.cite: E. J. W. Gibb, A History of Ottoman Poetry, vol. III (London: Luzac, 1904), ch. on Bâkî, Gibb's footnotes to the qasida

title: Key-Qubâd and Qahramân
greek: Persian Kay-Qubād; Qahramān ('hero')
short: Beside the sultan's justice even the legendary king Kay Qubad looks tyrannical; beside his anger the fury of the hero Qahraman is mildness.
body: Gibb's notes identify Key-Qubâd as the founder of the legendary Kayanian (Keyânî) dynasty of Persia, whose adventures are told in Firdawsī's Shāhnāma, and Qahramân as a legendary hero whom the kings of the fairies asked for help against the demons; his adventures fill the popular Qahramân-Nâma. In 1882 Gibb glosses Key-Qubâd as Dejoces, an identification he drops in 1904. The couplet pairs the two halves of kingship that panegyric always praises together: justice (adl) and terrifying wrath (kahr).

sources.cite: E. J. W. Gibb, Ottoman Poems Translated into English Verse in the Original Forms (London: Trübner, 1882), notes 176-177, p. 253
E. J. W. Gibb, A History of Ottoman Poetry, vol. III (London: Luzac, 1904), ch. on Bâkî, Gibb's footnotes 5-6 to the qasida

title: The 'Anqa of Mount Qaf
greek: Arabic ʿanqāʾ; Persian sīmurgh; Turkish zümrüdüanka
short: The sultan's power is the 'Anqa, the vast fabulous bird of Mount Qaf, which could pick up the sphere of heaven like a grain of seed.
body: The 'Anqa (Persian Sîmurg) is the great mythical bird of Near Eastern legend, said to nest on Mount Qaf, the mountain range that rings the world; Gibb's 1882 notes quote the cosmographer Qazwini's claim that it can carry off an elephant. In Sufi poetry, above all Attar's Conference of the Birds, it figures the unreachable divine. Here it is simply the measure of power: to such a bird the whole sphere of heaven is a single grain. Gibb's 1904 version makes the earth 'one bite' for 'the canqa of the Qaf'.

title: The sphere as a polo ball
greek: Persian chawgān ('polo stick'); Turkish çevgân; Arabic azal ('eternity without beginning')
short: In pre-eternity the sultan's hand struck the sphere with a polo stick, and it is still spinning from the blow.
body: Polo was a royal game in Persia, and the ball and stick (gûy u çevgân) are a favourite courtly image. Bâkî says that the sultan's might struck the ball of heaven in 'past eternity' (ezel, the timeless beginning when destinies were fixed), and 'that time is this time': the sky's turning is the continuing effect of that single blow. Gibb calls the idea extravagant and quotes a parallel from Hafiz, in which the sphere circles like a steed urged by the beloved's whip. It is another case of a fanciful cause given to a natural fact.

anchor: If yonder mouth be not the soul
title: The inset ghazel (tegazzül)
greek: Arabic taghazzul ('composing love lyric'); Turkish tegazzül, tecdîd-i matla'
short: Here the qasida turns into a love lyric addressed to a beloved, with a fresh rhyming opening couplet; Gibb marks where this ghazel begins and ends.
body: Ottoman qasidas often contain a ghazel, introduced with a new matla' (a couplet in which both lines rhyme). Gibb notes that the ghazel begins here and is addressed to an imaginary being, 'conceived either as an earthly beauty or as a divine ideal'. Its first conceit is the beloved's mouth, so tiny that it is invisible, and so like the soul, which is also hidden and is the source of the lover's life. The bird-heart that 'singeth' this lay in the sultan's garden of praise links the ghazel to the panegyric frame. Gibb marks the end of the ghazel at the couplet about earth's cries rising to the skies.

title: Syrians dancing to Hijaz: a double meaning
greek: Arabic Shāmī ('Syrian'; Persian shām 'evening'); Ḥijāz (region and musical mode); Turkish îhâm
short: The beloved's dark curls are 'Shâmîs', both Syrians and evening-dark things, who have tucked up their skirts to dance to Hijaz, a region and a musical mode.
body: Gibb's notes untangle a pun typical of Bâkî's fondness for îhâm (a word used in two senses at once). Shâmî means Syrian, and also, through Persian shâm 'evening', dark like evening, so it suits black hair. Hijâz is the region of Arabia with Mecca and Medina, the goal of pilgrims setting out from Syria, and also one of the modes (makam) of Ottoman music. So the curls tumbling over the cheek are Syrians girding up their robes for the journey to Hijaz, or dancers moving to the Hijaz mode. Gibb's 1882 note 85 gives the same musical pun for Iraq and Hijaz in another poem.

title: Sujûd and qiyâm: the flowers at prayer
greek: Arabic sujūd ('prostration'), qiyām ('standing')
short: Rose and jasmine bow in prostration before the beloved's cheek, and the upright cypress stands as worshippers stand in the ritual prayer.
body: Sujûd is the position in the Muslim ritual prayer (namaz) in which the forehead touches the ground; qiyâm is the upright standing position. Gibb explains the couplet: the rose and jasmine (the red and white of a lovely cheek) bend when the wind blows, but the poet says they prostrate themselves before a cheek fairer than themselves; the cypress, naturally erect, stands up in homage to a figure more graceful still. The symbols of beauty thus perform the prayer before the beloved. Gibb cites it as another example of hüsn-i ta'lîl. The religious language is bold, and it is one reason readers ask whether the beloved of the inset ghazel is human or divine.

title: 'Be! and it is': the universe
greek: Arabic kun fa-yakūn; Turkish kün fe-kân
short: God's creative command 'Be!' stands for the whole created world: the 'hall' of 'Be! and it is' resounds with love for the beloved.
body: The Qur'an says that when God decrees a thing, He says to it only 'Be!' and it is (2:117 and elsewhere). Gibb's note: kun, 'Be!', was God's fiat to creation, so 'the hall, BE! and it is' simply means the universe. The phrase was a commonplace of theology, Sufism and poetry for creation out of nothing. Here it gives the beloved's beauty a cosmic range: like the sun it fills the earth, and the whole of creation echoes with love of it.

title: The poet's signature couplet
greek: Arabic takhalluṣ ('pen-name'); Turkish mahlas; tâc ('crown')
short: Bâkî names himself: no nightingale sings as sweetly as he. Gibb calls this verse the 'taj or crown', after which the sultan is addressed again.
body: Every ghazel and qasida names its poet by his pen-name in a closing couplet. Bâkî's pen-name means 'Abiding' or 'Everlasting', which gives his boasts an extra edge. In a qasida this self-praise belongs to the fahriyye, the section in which the poet praises his own art, and it often asks for patronage. Gibb notes that this verse is the 'taj or crown', in which the poet mentions his own name, and that from here the sultan is addressed again. The nightingale (bülbül), lover of the rose, is the conventional figure for the poet.

title: Irem, the lost garden
greek: Arabic Iram dhāt al-ʿimād ('Iram of the pillars')
short: The world blooms under the sultan's beauty like Irem, the legendary garden-city that King Shaddad built to rival Paradise.
body: The Qur'an mentions 'Iram of the pillars, the like of which was never created in the lands' (89:6-8) among peoples destroyed for their pride. Later legend made it a terrestrial paradise built by King Shaddad, now lost somewhere in the Arabian desert, and in poetry Irem means simply a garden of perfect beauty. Gibb explains that the 'mead' here is the world of Islam and that the nightingales of the next line are poets, adding that under Süleyman Ottoman poetry reached its highest point.

title: The closing prayer and the silver candlestick
greek: Arabic duʿāʾ ('prayer'); Turkish duâ
short: The prayer section asks God to guard the taper of the sultan's life; Gibb himself was unsure what the silver candelabrum of dawn alludes to.
body: A qasida ends with a prayer for the person praised (duâ), usually 'so long as' some cosmic order lasts. Here it lasts as long as the dawn sets the sun-lamp on a silver candlestick (the white light of daybreak on the horizon). In 1882 Gibb thought 'some allusion lurks' in the couplet and guessed that Bâkî prays for the sultan to live to old age, until his face (the sun) shows a silver candelabrum, a white beard. He did not repeat the guess in 1904, translating the line plainly. The image of life as a candle threatened by the 'blast of doom' is conventional.

title: The sky as gold-inlaid steel
greek: Persian pūlād ('steel'); Turkish çelik ('steel'), bezm ('banquet')
short: The last couplet makes the cosmos the sultan's banquet: glory his companion, fortune his cupbearer, the sphere his goblet, the starry night a steel bowl inlaid with gold.
body: Gibb's note explains the final picture: the dark slate-blue night sky studded with stars is sometimes compared to steel inlaid with gold, the luxury metalwork (koftgari or damascening) of Ottoman and Persian workshops. The qasida thus ends where it began, with the night sky, but now the stars that opened the poem as festival lamps have become the decoration of the sultan's own wine-bowl. The banquet (bezm) and battle (rezm) are the two settings of royal praise, and Bâkî closes on the banquet.
